content.title: FOOD FACTS THAT SOUND {{MADE UP}} BUT ARE 100% TRUE
facts: **Pineapples** take almost two years to grow and actually flower before the fruit forms — it's one single fruit made of dozens of smaller fruits fused together.
**Pistachios** are so oil-rich that a pile of them can technically combust on their own if stored in a warm, poorly ventilated container — shipping companies classify raw ones as a mild fire risk.
**Carrots** were originally purple, not orange — the orange variety was bred in the Netherlands in the 1600s and simply became the one that stuck.
**Almonds** are technically not nuts at all — they're the seed found inside a fruit that looks like a fuzzy, dry peach.
**Bananas** are naturally slightly radioactive because of their potassium content — it's completely harmless, but it's a real, measurable effect scientists call the 'banana equivalent dose.'
**Nutmeg** contains a natural compound that, in large enough doses, can cause hallucinations — a fact discovered the hard way by prisoners in the 1800s who had nothing else to get a buzz from.
**Strawberries** aren't technically berries, but bananas are — in botany, a true berry needs seeds formed inside its flesh, which strawberries carry on the outside instead.
**Follow along** – for more daily health facts that sound fake but are completely real.
content.caption:
Some of these still feel unreal even after double-checking them. Take pineapples: each one actually starts as a cluster of over a hundred tiny flowers on a single stalk, and every flower contributes to one segment of the fruit you eventually cut into — that's why the surface looks like a honeycomb of little eyes. Pistachios are so dense in natural oils that heat building up inside a packed, humid shipping container can trigger spontaneous combustion, which is why bulk shipments are legally handled like a flammable good. And nutmeg contains myristicin, a compound your liver converts into something chemically similar to mild hallucinogens when eaten in large amounts — in tiny baking quantities it's completely harmless, but whole nutmegs were historically hoarded and even smuggled because of this effect. Wild stuff, and every bit of it checks out.

This is the kind of everyday food trivia @smarthealthfix loves digging into, alongside the usual topics of nutrition, common symptoms, organ function, and the small daily habits that actually move the needle. Our mission is to make nutrition feel a little more fascinating, not just another list of rules to follow.
